title: Security Engineer: Review a Vendor Access Proposal
prompt: Fictional Maple Logistics needs a vendor to diagnose a reporting failure tomorrow. Review this request: "Create one shared administrator account, email its password to the vendor team, allow access to all customer records, and remove it after the project." A sanitized test environment exists. Company policy requires named accounts, approved scope, an expiry date, and reviewable access records. Propose a workable revision and defend its tradeoffs; do not implement access.
blurb: Turn an overbroad vendor request into scoped, approved access with a clear verification and removal plan.

rubric.label: Understand the task and exposure
rubric.description: Connects requested privileges and data to a diagnostic need.

anchors.0: Approves unrestricted shared access or blocks all help without investigating need.
anchors.2: Flags shared admin access and broad data exposure and asks what the vendor needs.
anchors.4: Separates configuration, sample data, and residual production questions; ranks risks by the actual diagnostic task.

rubric.label: Design a bounded path
rubric.description: Uses the stated policy to build an operable access proposal.

anchors.0: Emails a shared password or relies on an undefined project end to remove access.
anchors.2: Proposes named, scoped accounts with an explicit expiry and access records.
anchors.4: Starts with sanitized testing, sets least necessary permissions and a timed owner-approved production exception only if justified, with a revocation owner.

rubric.label: Verify usefulness and removal
rubric.description: Makes the access decision reviewable and tests both task completion and closure.

anchors.0: Assumes creating controls proves the failure is fixed or access has ended.
anchors.2: Defines a diagnostic success check and confirms account expiry.
anchors.4: Names evidence of session scope, result, remaining uncertainty, and actual revocation; explains how to adjust if the initial permissions are insufficient.

reference.scenario: Fictional Maple Logistics needs a vendor to diagnose a reporting failure tomorrow. Review this request: "Create one shared administrator account, email its password to the vendor team, allow access to all customer records, and remove it after the project." A sanitized test environment exists. Company policy requires named accounts, approved scope, an expiry date, and reviewable access records. Propose a workable revision and defend its tradeoffs; do not implement access.

facts.value: The vendor says it needs report configuration and an example failure, not complete customer histories. A sanitized example reproduces most but not all failures.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks what data or permissions the vendor needs

facts.value: The service owner can approve a four-hour, monitored production session if the sanitized environment cannot answer a specific question. The project end date is unknown.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about approval, urgency, or exceptions

model_points: The proposal conflicts with every stated account-control requirement. Explain the failure mode of each issue instead of reciting a checklist: shared identity weakens attribution, admin scope exceeds diagnostic need, and an unknown project end leaves access open.

Use the sanitized environment first. If a particular failure cannot be reproduced there, ask the owner to approve a bounded production session with named identities, minimal scope, time limit, and appropriate access records.

Define the diagnostic deliverable, who supervises production access, and who verifies expiry or revocation. Monitor only authorized work; do not introduce secret employee surveillance or promise controls eliminate all risk.

probes.question: How would you let tomorrow's diagnosis proceed while addressing the stated risks?

probes.trigger: candidate proposes a temporary account without an expiry
probes.question: The project end date is unknown. What exact condition closes this access?

fair_alternatives: A supervised screen-sharing diagnosis led by an authorized employee can be reasonable if it limits data exposure and preserves a record.
Read-only production access may be justified for a specific unresolved question; it still needs a named identity, approval, expiry, and minimum data scope.
red_flags: Approves unrestricted shared access or blocks all help without investigating need.
Emails a shared password or relies on an undefined project end to remove access.
Assumes creating controls proves the failure is fixed or access has ended.
follow_ups: Rewrite the vendor request in six sentences with scope, identity, time limit, approval, evidence, and closure.
reference.exemplar_answer: I would replace shared administrator access with named, expiring accounts for a sanitized diagnostic environment. The vendor would receive the failing example and needed configuration only. If a specific failure remains unresolved, I would bring that question to the service owner for a four-hour monitored production session, using the narrowest useful permissions. The request would name the supervisor, diagnostic output, and person verifying access removal.

interviewer_notes: Act as the service owner defending the deadline. Ask about one operational tradeoff after the revision. Do not reward product-specific tooling or require blanket refusal. Use only supplied facts; say when something is unknown. Accept plain language and equivalent approaches. Assess the demonstrated decisions, not accent, confidence, credentials, or access to particular employers. This is a fictional exercise; do not imply real actions were performed.

learning_drills.title: Rewrite an access request
learning_drills.prompt: Rewrite the vendor request in six sentences with scope, identity, time limit, approval, evidence, and closure. This is self-guided practice; no model assessment is performed.
checklist: Tie permissions to a diagnostic need
Identify an approver and revocation owner
Specify how success and removal will be verified
